The defence was tried by ENGLISCH at Vienna 1 882, by BLACKBURN£ in 1 883 ('Not much good comes of this' he wrote), and was pioneered by NIMZOWITSCH around 1 9 1 4. The most popular reply for White is the RUBINSTEIN VARIATI"

The continuation 5 . . . gxf3 6 Qxf3 Qf6 7 e5 Qxe5 8 d3 Bh6 9 Nc3 Ne7 I 0 Bd2 Nbc6 1 1 Rae l was regarded as favouring White until 1 858 when 'W.S.' of Milwaukee discovered an adequate reply, 1 1 . . . Qf5, a move introduced to master play in the 6th match game Kolisch Paulsen. 1 86 1 ,"
Fishbein, The Exchange French Comes to Life, chapter 'The Uhlmann Gambit'; Wikipedia, 'Wolfgang Uhlmann' (re-verified 2026-06-11): 'one of the world's leading experts on the French Defence'.
Moskalenko, Even More Flexible French, chapter on King's Indian Attack / Barcza System; Wikipedia, 'Gedeon Barcza' (re-verified 2026-06-11): 'The Barcza System is named after him.'

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Alekhine–Chatard Attack on the French Defence': "Chatard-Alekhine Attack, or Albin Attack, 1 22 1 , a popular line in the FRENCH DEFENCE originated by ALBIN in the 1 890s and analysed a few years later by the French player Eugene Chatard ( 1 850- 1 924). His analysis may have influenced ALEKHINE to play it against FAHRNI at Mannheim 1 9 1 4, and so it is sometimes called the Alekhine Attack."

Moskalenko, Even More Flexible French, chapter on Kortchnoi's 'wedge' against the French Super Gambit; corroborated by ChessBase, 'The Korchnoi Gambit against the French' (Collins). The cited book spells the surname 'Kortchnoi'.

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Balogh Defense': "Balogh Defence. 236 or 259, an old opening line given by coz10 (I e4 d6 2 d4 f5), played in the 5th match game Kieseritzky-Horwitz, 1 846, much analysed by Balogh in Wiener Schach=eitung, 1 930."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Keres Variation': "Keres Variation. An excellent openings analyst, KERES originated several important lines, and strengthened many variations by his analysis and praxis: 20 in the ENGLISH OPENING; 31 in the same opening, known from a game Euwe-Bogoljubow, Mahrisch-Ostrau 1 923, popularized by Keres in the 1 950s, but LAsKER used a similar idea at St Petersburg 1 909; 30 I and 32 1 in the NIMZO-INIJIAN DEFENCE, the second being played in Stahlberg-Keres. Bad Nauheim 1 936; 388 in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE, as Pach man- Keres, Moscow 1 94 7; 400 in the KING'S INDIAN DEFENCE played by Keres in the 1 960s; 459 in the SIC"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Steinitz Variation': "Steinitz Variation, 74 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT ACCEPTED, as in the 9th game of the first world championship match in 1 886, Zukertort-Steinitz, and also Pillsbury-Steinitz, St Petersburg 1 895-6. In each case the position was reached by transposition, for STEINITZ did not like accepting the gambit on the second move. His idea was to exploit White's ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN. Also 566 in the SICILIAN DEFENCE, tried by Steinitz in his l 2th match game against ANDERSSEN in 1 866 but played only rarely, e .g. by TARTAKOWER, after whom it is sometimes named; 5 7 1 in the CARO-KANN DEFENCE, suggested but "

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Carrera Gambit': "Carrera Gambit, 1 1 1 5, one of four queen moves (after 1 e4 e5 2 f4 exf4) examined by CARRERA; all have fallen out of use except 1 1 75, the BREYER GAMBIT, which sometimes bears Carrera's name."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Stamma Gambit': "Stamma Gambit. 1 1 76. a method of playing the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted, recommended by STAMMA in 1 745 but supported by no master. It is sometimes called the Calvi Variation, or Rook's Pawn Gambit."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Villemson Gambit': "Villemson Gambit, 1 1 1 3 in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted, sometimes called the Steinitz Gambit (perhaps because of its resemblance to 6 1 4, but STEINITZ did play it in a consultation game in 1 880), or the Krause, Polerio, or Rosentreter Gambit. Martin Villemson ( 1 897- 1 933) of Parnu, Estonia, editor of the chess magazine Eesti Maleilm, played it in the first International Correspondence Tournament of the Deutsche Schachzeitung. He was a strong correspondence player and may well have inspired KERES to try that activity, in which they overlapped."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Fischer Defense': "Fischer Defence, 1 1 20, a variation of the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted advocated by STAMMA in 1 745 and by FISCHER ('a high-class waiting move') in the American Chess Quarterly in the early 1 960s. Black reserves the option of dcf ending his gambit pawn while avoiding the hazards of the KIESERITZKY and ALLGAIER GAMBITS. Compare HECKER DEFENCE, 1 1 74, which is, perhaps, a less commendable way to achieve the same object."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Schallopp Defense': "Schallopp Defence, 1 1 26 in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted, played Thorold- Schallopp, Hereford 1 885, but popular with the Russian player llya Stepanovich Shumov ( 1 8 1 9-8 1 ) much earlier. For example, a game Jaenisch Shumov, in this line, was in the Illustrated London News, 20 April 1 857."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Cunningham Defense': "Cunningham Gambit, 1 1 21, a line in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted that was evolved c. 1 706 by the Scottish historian Alexander CUNNINGHAM. After 4 Bc4 he advocated 4 . . . Bh4 + , probably a sound continuation, but superseded by 4 . . . Nf6 as recommended by SCHLECHTER in the eighth edition of the HANDBUCH, 1 912- 16."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Döry Defence': "Dory Defence, 356 and 429, pioneered by Ladislaus Dory, an Austrian Baron, in 1 923, and played with some international success by KERES who won a small tournament at Vienna 1 937 in which all games had to begin with this opening. In 1943 Dory was sentenced to death by the Nazis for sedition, but was released from prison by Allied troops in 1945."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Santasiere's Folly': "Santasiere's Folly, 1 285, a relative of the ORANG UTAN OPENING (6). At Portsmouth 1 923, already assured of first prize, ALEKHINE played this opening against Drewitt. Later i t was taken up by Anthony Edward Santasiere ( 1 904--77), a colourful American player, who tried it against KASHDAN in the US championship, 1 938, and subsequently published analysis in the Chess Correspondent."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Schlechter Variation': "Schlechter Variation. 1 00, 1 08, 37 1 , or 375, combination of KING'S INDIAN and SLAV DEFENCES, played by ALAPIN against TARRASCH at Nuremberg 1 896, by SCHLECHTER in his match with LASKER, 1 9 1 0, and now a standard line (see LEVENFISH; NAJDORF; PROTECTED PASSED PAWN); 1 22 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined, sometimes called the Lodi: Variation, or Rubinstein Attack, i ntroduced in the game Schlechter-Duz-Khotimirsky, Prague 1 908, and usually regarded as the best way for White to attack the TARRASCH DEFENCE. The variation was tested in a FIXED OPENINGS tournament, Budapest 1 9 1 2."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Steinitz Attack': "1 245, variation in the FRENCH DEFENCE given by cozIO and played six times ( + 4 = I - I ) by Steinitz at the Vienna tournament of 1 882."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Gurgenidze Variation': "Gurgenidze Variation, 463 as Gurgenidze-Furman, USSR Championship 1 967; 495. as Keres B. I. Gurgenidze, USSR championship 1 959, both in the SICILIAN DEFENCE; 580 in the CARO- KANN DEFENCE, played by GURGENIDZE in the 1 970s after experimenting with 3 . . . b5 in the 1 960s; 1 277 in the ROBATSCH DEFENCE, as Klovan-Gurgenidzc, Omsk 1 965."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Kondratiyev Variation': "Kondratiyev Variation, 1 1 86 in the FRENCH DEFENCE, an idea of the Soviet player Pavel Evseyevich Kondratiyev ( 1 924-84 )."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Robatsch Defence': "Robatsch Defence. 1 276, also known as the King's Fianchetto Dcf ence, the Modern Defence, or the Ujtelky Defence. Known since the 1 6th century this defence was rarely played until the middle of the 20th century, when i t was used by the Austrian grandmaster (and orchidologist) Karl Robatsch ( 1 928 - ). Play usually leads to the PIRC- ROBA TSCH SYSTEM although other options are open to Black, as, for example, the GURGENIDZE VARIATION, 1 277."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Gurgenidze Defense': "Gurgenidze Variation, 463 as Gurgenidze-Furman, USSR Championship 1 967; 495. as Keres B. I. Gurgenidze, USSR championship 1 959, both in the SICILIAN DEFENCE; 580 in the CARO- KANN DEFENCE, played by GURGENIDZE in the 1 970s after experimenting with 3 . . . b5 in the 1 960s; 1 277 in the ROBATSCH DEFENCE, as Klovan-Gurgenidzc, Omsk 1 965."

Edward Winter, 'Géza Maróczy' (chesshistory.com) / 'Kings, Commoners and Knaves' (1999); Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., 1992). First recognised master game: Swiderski–Maróczy, Monte Carlo 1904.

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Smith–Morra Gambit': "Smith-Morra Gambit, 457, the MORRA GAMBIT, practised by the American player Kenneth Ray Smith ( 1 930 - )."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Marshall Variation': "Marshall Variation. 560, line in the SICILIAN DEFENCE given by JAENISCH; 8 5 I in the SPANISH FOUR KNIGHTS GAME, introduced in Mar6czy-Marshall, Monte Carlo 1 904; I 065 in the PETROFF DEFENCE, an old line played, for instance, by STAUNTON in the London 1 8 5 1 tournament, but used by MARSHALL throughout his life, alert to the possibility of the MARSHALL TRAP; 1 195, FRENCH DEFENCE variation of dubious merit, played at Amsterdam 1 85 1 ; 1 52, STONEWALL Variation."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Brentano Defense': "Brentano Defence, 8 1 1 , a dubious reply to the SPANISH OPENING dating from 1 900, when Brentano published his analysis in the Wiener Schachzeitung; 1 1 39, in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted from the second edition of the HANDBUCH. Franz Clemens Honoratus Hermann Josef Brentano ( 1 838- 1 9 1 7) . a well-known German philosopher who lived in Vienna, frequently published analyses of the openings."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Pollock's Defense to the Ruy Lopez': "Pollock Defence, 765, an uncommon line in the SPANISH OPENING, used by the English master William Henry Krause Pollock ( 1 859-96) against LASKER and BURN. Writing in the Baltimore News about the ALAPIN DEFENCE (766), Pollock said, ' It is even worse than my move, if only because less ridiculous.'"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Bird Defense': "Bird Defence, 773, reply to the SPANISH OPENING given in the first edition of the HANDBUCH, 1 843. Pioneered by BIRD, e.g. against ANDERSSEN in 1 854, and used on occasion by grandmasters such as TARRASCH, SPASSKY, and MALANYUK, this defence has not gained wide acceptance."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Steinitz Defense': "Steinitz Defence. 776 in the SPANISH OPENING, practised by STEINITZ in the 1 890s. His idea was to disturb Black's pawn formation as little as possible and, perhaps, to maintain the pawn at e5. The latter object is seldom achieved: for example, to avoid the TARRASCH TRAP, 780, Black must play 7 . . . exd4, still, however, with a playable game. Masters usually arrive at the Steinitz Defence by transposition, e.g. 3 . . . Nf6 4 0-0 d6, thus avoiding the continuation 3 . . . d6 4 d4 Bd7 5 Nc3 Nf6 6 Bxc6 Bxc6 7 Qd3 when White threatens to gain advantage by castling on the queen's-side. This defenc"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Steinitz Gambit': "Steinitz Gambit, 6 1 4 in the VIENNA GAME, introduced successfully in the game Steinitz-Neumann, Dundee 1 867; 1 1 1 3, the VILLEMSON GAMBIT."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Hanham Variation': "Hanham Variation, 1 022 in the PHILIDOR DEFENCE. At the New York 1 889 tournament the American player James Moore Hanham ( 1 840- 1 923) reintroduced the LORD VARIATION with a superior idea in mind: he had devised a way by which Black could defend the e-pawn and thus maintain a DEFENSIVE CENTRE."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Alapin's Opening': "Alapin Opening, 67 1 , played with the intention of continuing 3 r4. Analysed by Carl Mayerhofer ( 1 828- 1 9 1 3) in Schachzeitung, 1 849, this uncommon opening was played by Ljubojevic at Groningen 1 970 and (with transposition, i.e. 2 f4 exf4 3 Ne2) by Alapin at Manchester 1 890. At one time it was jokingly called the HIPPOPOTAMUS GAME."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Philidor Variation': "Philidor Variation, 643, sometimes called the Classical Attack, in the BISHOP'S OPENING, given by Ruy LÓPEZ, and advocated by PHILIDOR as the proper way to build a PAWN CENTRE. The variation had an extraordinarily long run during which STAMMA's continuation, 3 . . . Nf6 4 d4 cxd4 5 c5 d5, was thought to favour White. Eventually improvements for Black were found: 6 exf6 dxc4 7 Qh5 {}- {) (PRATT, 1 825); 6 Bb3 Ne4 7 cxd4 Qh4 (CALVI, 1 842). Also 455 and 565, Philidor's replies to the SICILIAN DEFENCE."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Blackburne Shilling Gambit': "Blackburne Shilling Gambit, 935, a fruitful source of income for BLACKBURNE when playing cafe visitors, the usual stake being one shilling. Black's third move may not be good enough for master chess but it is not an outright error and cannot be refuted by violence. A quiet continuation such as 4 0-0 maintains White's lead in development. The line continues to catch victims, including two in successive rounds at Blackpool 1 987."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Blackmar–Diemer Gambit': "Blackmar-Diemer Gambit, 55 or 22 1 , a variation of the BLACKMAR GAMBIT. lgnacy Popiel ( 1 863 -1 94 1 ) noted in Deutsches Wochenschach, 1 893, that the Blackmar Gambit (I d4 d5 2 c4 dxe4 3 f3) could be answered effectively by 3 . . . c5; instead of 3 f3 he recommended 3 Nc3, which he called the Polish Gambit in honour of his native land . In 1 932 the German player Emil Josef Diemer ( 1 908 90), following Popicl's analysis, 3 Nc3 Nf6, advocated the continuation 4 f3. The gambit thus modified (which may occur by transposition when the game begins I d4 Nf6) has been played occasionally by gran"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Colle System': "Colle System, 1 309, the opening moves, for White, Pd4, Nf3, Pc3, Nbd2, Pc3, and Bd3; White prepares an advance of the c-pawn thus opening the diagonal for the DARK BISHOP. Play frequently begins 1 d4 d5 2 Nf3 Nf6 3 e3 c5 (225), but Black has other ways of defending: for example, the game Ahues-Alekhine, San Remo 1 930, opened 1 d4 Nf6 2 Nf3 b6 3 e3 Bb7 4 Nbd2 c6 5 Bd3 c5 6 c3. The system made its first appearance in the 1 890s when it was used by Black in the CHIGORIN VARIATION (148). Masters began to use the system for White around 1 900, and in this form COLLE made it his speciality in the"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Flohr Variation': "Flohr Variation, 33 and 44 in the ENGLISH OPENING, the first recommended by ALEKHINE in 1 926 as a refutation of 2 NB, the second introduced by NIMZOWITSCH and taken up successfully by FLOHR in 1 933; 72 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT ACCEPTED, played by Flohr against RESHEVSKY at Nottingham 1 936 ('seems to rehabilitate the entire line of defence' -Alekhine): 376 and 379 in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE; 466 in the SICILIAN DEFENCE, played by Flohr several times at Nottingham and Moscow in 1 936; 574 in the CARO- KANN DEFENrE, an idea of OPOCENSKY's played twice by Flohr at Moscow 1935: 1 27 1 in the ALEKHINE "

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Levenfish Variation': "Levenfish Variation. 132, a recommendation by LEVENFISH made in the Russian Yearbook, 1 937, in which he gave a 53-page analysis of the QUEEN ' S GAMBIT; 383, line in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE abandoned because of the reply 8 e5; 884, a colourful but possibly unsound sacrifice in the EVANS GAMBIT."
Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Smyslov Variation': "377 in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE, favoured by Smyslov in the 1 950s, and 386, a similar variation;"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Hromádka System': "Hromadka Defence, 278, sometimes called the Loose Gambit, or Benoni Deferred. It was introduced by the Czech master Karel Hromadka ( 1 887-1 956) in the Piest'any tournament, 1 922. The play that follows often leads to the MODERN BENONI."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Jerome Gambit': "Jerome Gambit, 930, an unsound gambit suitable only for social chess. It appeared first in American Chess Journal, 1 876. recommended by Alonzo Wheeler Jerome (l 834 - 1 902) or Pax ton, I llinois."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Neumann Defense': "Neumann Defence, 1 1 52, a line in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted introduced by NEUMANN around 1 870, leading to a game with about level chances."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Konstantinopolsky Opening': "Konstantinopolsky Opening, 1 0 1 3, introduced to master play in the game Konstantinopolsky-Ragozin, team championship, Moscow 1 956."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Zaitsev Variation': "Zaitsev Variation, 543 in the SICILIAN DEFENCE; 772 in the SPANISH OPENING, recommended in 1 973 and 1 968 respectively by the Soviet player Igor Arkadyevich Zaitsev ( 1 938 - ). Sometimes used for the LENZERHEIDE VARIATION, 747."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Duras Variation': "Duras Variation, 2 1 5, a sound line, sometimes called the Moscow Variation, in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined; if 5 Bh4 Black can reply 5 . . . dxc4 or 5 . . . Bb4 + and 6 . . . dxc4, and White cannot respond with Pe2-e4. Another Queen's Gambit line, 1 89, introduced in the game Duras-Balla, Breslau 1 9 1 2. Also 695 and 79 1 , outmoded lines in the SPANISH OPENING, and 687, the KERES VARIATION and 75 1 , the KHOLMOV VARIATION, in the same opening."
Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Flohr Variation': "574 in the CARO- KANN DEFENrE, an idea of OPOCENSKY's played twice by Flohr at Moscow 1935"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Soldatenkov Variation': "Soldatenkov Variation, 1 077 in the KING'S GAMBIT Declined, a line given by LOPEZ in 1 56 1 but not taken seriously until played at Carlsbad 1 907 by MARSHALL. The idea came from Vasily V. Soldatenkov, a Russian military attache of the Tsarist times."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Knorre Variation': "708, a dubious line in the SPANISH OPENING played in the 1 870s by the Russian-born astronomer Victor Knorrc ( 1 840 - 1 9 1 9)"

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Furman Variation': "Furman Variation, 69 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT ACCEPTED. Beginning with 6 Qe2, FURMAN'S plan is to play dxc5 (without allowing a queen exchange on d I ) followed by Pe3-e4-e5."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Hübner Variation': "Hubner Variation, 3 1 8 in the NIMZO-INDIAN DEFENCE as Najdorf-Hubner, Wijk aan Zee 1 97 1 . The idea i s to follow with Pd7-d6 and leave White with DOUBLED PAWNS."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'McDonnell Gambit': "McDonnell Gambit, 1 1 29 in the KING'S GAMBIT Accepted, successfully introduced by McDONNELL in the first game of his third match against HOURDONNAIS. This alternative to the MUZIO GAMBIT, 1 1 38, is regarded as a less effective choice, but it has not been tested thoroughly."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Colman Variation': "Colman Variation, 958, a standard line, also known as the Bogoljubow Variation, in the TWO KNIGHTS DEFENCE. The English player Eugene Ernest Colman ( 1 878-1 964) discovered and analysed the variation while in a Japanese internment camp, 1 942-5."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Riumin Variation': "Riumin Variation. 346 in the QUEEN'S INDIAN DEFENCE, analysed by Nikolai Nikolayevich Riumin ( 1 908-42), ALATORTSEV, and LILIENTHAL. Also 538, the MOSCOW VARIATION of the SICILIAN DEFENCE."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Lasker Defence': "886, played in the game ChigorinLasker, St Petersburg 1 895 - 6, and usually regarded as the most solid way of defending the EVANS GAMBIT Accepted."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Mikenas Variation': "Mikenas Variation, 285, a sharp attacking line in the MODERN BENONI espoused by MIKENAS from the mid- 1 950s; 1 257 in the ALEKHINE DEFEl'iCE, played in a 1 948 match game Nezhmetdinov-Mikenas. Also 283, the PAWN STORM VARIATION, which may lead to 285."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Bellon Gambit': "Bellon Gambit, 28, in the ENGLISH OPENING, played in the early 1 970s by the Spanish Grandmaster Juan Manuel Bellon ( 1 950 - ) ."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Gurgenidze Variation': "Gurgenidze Variation, 463 as Gurgenidze-Furman, USSR Championship 1 967; 495. as Keres B. I. Gurgenidze, USSR championship 1 959, both in the SICILIAN DEFENCE; 580 in the CARO- KANN DEFENCE, played by GURGENIDZE in the 1 970s after experimenting with 3 . . . b5 in the 1 960s; 1 277 in the ROBATSCH DEFENCE, as Klovan-Gurgenidzc, Omsk 1 965."

Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Harrwitz Attack': "Harrwitz Attack. 1 70, a QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined variation favoured by HARRWITZ and also by RUBINSTEIN, after whom it is sometimes named. Harrwitz played it successfully in matches, notably in 1 853 against LOWENTHAL and in 1 858 against MORPHY, who considered the l ine so strong that he then avoided the Queen's Gambit, preferring the DUTCH DEFENCE, 247. In his world championship matches of 1 978 and 1 98 1 KORCHNOI employed the Harrwitz Attack in its current form, after 4 Nf3 Be7. See games under HARRWITZ, MACKENZIE, and PHILIDOR SACRIFICE."
